name: Sercer decortication rhinoplasty

lead: Decortication of the nose, associated with the surgeon Sercer, is an early form of open rhinoplasty. The skin is temporarily separated from the nasal framework through a columellar (and slot) incision so the surgeon can work on the tip, dorsum and septum under direct view.

Its appearance payoff is the same as that of modern open rhinoplasty: more precise reshaping of the nasal tip and bridge. The approach was described in the 1950s and later refined and popularised by other surgeons; today's external rhinoplasty descends from it.

paras: It is done by a surgeon under anesthesia. Patients researching it in looksmaxxing settings generally encounter it as the historical root of open rhinoplasty, which is discussed alongside closed rhinoplasty when choosing an approach.
As with any rhinoplasty, risks include swelling that can last a year or more, a visible columellar scar, contour deformities and the need for revision in a minority of cases. Smoking impairs healing.

lead: Sercer decortication rhinoplasty, also called decortication of the nose, is a historic open approach to nasal surgery. A 1975 paper describes it as combining extranasal and intranasal access: the skin is temporarily removed from the framework of the nasal tip and dorsum through a columellar and slot incision, which allows surgery on the nasal pyramid and septum under direct visual control.[1]

For someone seeking a refined nose, the technique matters because it opened the way to precise work on the tip and bridge with the skin lifted away. Surgical histories credit Sercer with describing the method in 1957, with Padovan and Goodman later popularising the open approach in the 1970s.[2]

Clinical literature on the specific technique is mostly historical. A later paper reported that the external approach had been revived over the previous decade for cosmetic and functional septorhinoplasty and other nasal conditions.[3]
infobox: Performed by a surgeon under anesthesia

paras: The procedure is characterised as temporary decortication: the soft-tissue envelope is lifted off the cartilaginous and bony framework through a columellar incision plus a slot incision, then redraped.[1] The aim described in the original literature was to perform a wide range of interventions on the nasal pyramid and septum under visual inspection.[1]

Open approaches began with Rethi in 1934, using an incision across the columella. Sercer described decortication of the nose in 1957, Padovan refined the approach in the 1970s when closed surgery was standard, and Goodman helped popularise it later in the decade.[2] Gunter reported in 1987 that open access suited revision cases.[2] By the early 1990s, external rhinoplasty was being used for septorhinoplasty and for rhinologic problems such as septal perforation and rhinophyma.[3]

Open approaches give better visualisation and easier cartilage grafting, while closed approaches involve less dissection, less swelling and no external scar. Systematic reviews cited on Wikipedia found no significant long-term difference in functional or aesthetic outcomes, with choice depending on surgeon experience and anatomy.[2]
General rhinoplasty risks include prolonged swelling, contour deformities and revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations; smoking impairs healing.[2]
No studies found for outcomes of the specific Sercer technique in a modern sense; published items are a 1975 technique description[1] and a 1992 review of the broader external approach.[3]
